**Title:** 0.5.0 decodes 12–18% slower than 23cacbb across all prompt sizes: 36% more draft tokens proposed, 6 points lower acceptance

## Summary

**What we did.** We run a coding agent against Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Radeon 8060S, gfx1151,
128 GB unified), served by gufo in its runtime image, and we record every request the engine reports. We moved
from a development build to 0.5.0 on 3 October and kept running the same workload.

**What we see.** 0.5.0 sustains **12 to 18% less decode throughput** than the build before it, at every prompt
size. The 0.5.0 release notes state a timing regression of at most 0.4% from the project's own checks, so this
looks unintended rather than a known trade.

**What seems to cause it.** In the same requests, 0.5.0 proposes **36% more speculative draft tokens** and
accepts **6.1 percentage points fewer** of them. Prompt caching is not implicated and in fact improved.

**What we are asking.** Is the speculation change in 0.5.0 intended to propose longer drafts, and is the lower
acceptance expected? If not, the draft-length policy looks like the place to look.

**We are staying on 0.5.0.** It closed the tool-call defect we reported in
https://github.com/gufo-org/gufo/issues/304, which was ending whole runs for us, and that is worth far more to us than decode speed. This is a report, not a complaint.

## Environment

- gufo `0.5.0` (reports `gufo version 0.5.0 (23cacbb)`), runtime image pinned by digest, Podman, ROCm in-image
- Compared against the development build `b722a61`, same image family, same host
- Ryzen AI Max+ 395 / Radeon 8060S (`gfx1151`), 128 GB unified memory, Ubuntu 26.04
- Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, Unsloth `UD-Q4_K_XL`, with the shared `Q8_0` MTP head
- `--speculative mtp`, `--draft-tokens 7`, `--context 131072`, `--sessions 1`, `--prefill-chunk 512`
- Identical model, quantisation, flags, client and workload on both builds

## What we measured

The full write-up, including the query, is public here:
https://github.com/boxabirds/awesome-local-ai/blob/main/docs/reports/strategic-insights/2026-10-07-gufo-0.5.0-decodes-slower.md

Decode throughput is token-weighted: total generated tokens divided by total decode seconds, so a long request
counts for more than a short one. Figures come from the per-request accounting gufo itself reports
(`decode_tps`, `generated_tokens`, `prompt_tokens`, `cached_tokens`, `draft_accepted`, `draft_proposed`).

Pooled it is 47.0 → 42.2 tok/s. A pooled figure can hide a difference in workload, so here it is cut by prompt
size, which is the obvious confound:

| prompt tokens | `b722a61` | `0.5.0` | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| under 30k | 50.4 tok/s | 41.7 tok/s | −17.3% |
| 30k–60k | 51.2 tok/s | 42.1 tok/s | −17.8% |
| 60k–100k | 49.9 tok/s | 42.1 tok/s | −15.6% |
| 100k and over | 48.4 tok/s | 42.7 tok/s | −11.8% |

Request counts: 15,023 on 0.5.0, 12,265 on `b722a61`, across four buckets in both.

**0.5.0 is slower in every bucket.** A difference in what the runs happened to be doing would not produce a
consistent deficit across all four.

## What seems to cause it

The same requests, summarised:

| | `b722a61` | `0.5.0` |
|---|---|---|
| speculative draft acceptance | **79.5%** | **73.4%** |
| draft tokens proposed per request | 444.9 | **607.6** |
| cached prompt tokens per request | 63,159 | 67,720 |
| prompt tokens per request | 66,527 | 68,711 |

0.5.0 proposes about **36% more** draft tokens per request and accepts a **smaller share** of them. Speculative
decoding pays off only when drafts are accepted; proposing more while accepting proportionally less means more
verification work for each accepted token, which is what a decode-rate drop looks like.

**Prompt caching is not the cause**, and improved: 0.5.0 reuses 98.6% of each prompt against 94.9% before
(67,720 of 68,711 tokens, against 63,159 of 66,527). Whatever the cache changes in 0.5.0 did, they did not cost
this.

Draft length is adaptive, so proposing more is not a fault by itself — the engine lengthens drafts when
acceptance looks good. It is the pairing of more proposed *and* a lower accepted share that costs throughput.

## One other difference, possibly deliberate

The older build's decode rate falls as the prompt grows (50.4 → 48.4 tok/s from the smallest bucket to the
largest). 0.5.0's does not (41.7 → 42.7). If 0.5.0 traded peak speed for flatness at long context on purpose,
that would explain the shape, and we could not find it stated in the notes.

## What we are not claiming

- This is an observational comparison of two sets of runs on one machine, not a controlled A/B with identical
  inputs. The defence is the bucketed cut: the deficit holds across all four prompt sizes.
- One machine, one model, one quantisation, one speculation mode. We do not know whether it holds elsewhere.
- Decode speed is not what we rank engines on, and 0.5.0 is the best-scoring gufo configuration we have run.

## How to reproduce the measurement

For any two builds, over a workload with the same model and flags, group the per-request figures gufo already
logs by prompt size and compare, rather than pooling:

- decode: `sum(generated_tokens) / sum(generated_tokens / decode_tps)` per bucket
- acceptance: `sum(draft_accepted) / sum(draft_proposed)` per build
- cache reuse: `sum(cached_tokens) / sum(prompt_tokens)` per build

A long agentic workload makes the difference easy to see because almost every request reuses a large cached
prefix and then generates for a while, so decode dominates the wall clock.
